name: Coffee for skin / Cold brew

image.caption: Study for The Coffee House by Alson Skinner Clark

lead: Appearance communities promote coffee and cold brew, drunk or applied topically, for healthier-looking skin and looks in general.

Cold brew is made by steeping coarse grounds in cold or room-temperature water for about 4 to 24 hours and has lower titratable acidity than hot coffee. A 2017 umbrella review found coffee generally safe at usual intakes. The sources reviewed do not address skin, topical use, cellulite or under-eye effects of coffee.

paras: People drink coffee or cold brew daily, and some use coffee grounds or cold brew as a topical scrub or under-eye treatment. It is usually part of a wider skincare or diet routine.
Caffeine can cause anxiety or sleep disruption at high intakes, and pregnancy limits apply.

social.title: Cold brew coffee yummier and better for your brain

angle.text: Appearance communities drink coffee and cold brew, or apply it topically, aiming for healthier-looking skin. Coffee has general safety and health research behind it; skin effects have not been studied in the sources reviewed.

lead: Coffee for skin / cold brew refers to claims in appearance communities about coffee, including cold brew, and skin or looks, whether by drinking or topical use.

Cold brew is made by steeping coarse grounds in cold or room-temperature water for about 4 to 24 hours; research reports lower titratable acidity than hot coffee.[1] A 2017 umbrella review found coffee generally safe at usual intakes.[2] The sources reviewed do not discuss skin, topical use, cellulite or under-eye effects of coffee.

paras: Cold water extracts fewer of the acidic oils found in hot-brewed coffee, linked to lower acidity and astringency (Rao and Fuller, 2018).[1] Caffeine extracts more slowly in cold water.[1]

Coffee is associated with lower all-cause and cardiovascular mortality and lower type 2 diabetes risk, with possible increased fracture risk in women and pregnancy concerns.[2] Unfiltered coffee can raise LDL cholesterol.[2]
No studies found on coffee or cold brew for skin appearance in the sources reviewed.
